topic: Spot the hype / peptides your body makes: the placebo effect and the brain's own opioid peptides. Levine, Gordon & Fields, Lancet 1978 (PMID 80579): after impacted wisdom-tooth (third molar) extraction, double-blind naloxone vs placebo; placebo responders' pain relief was reversed by naloxone, nonresponders unaffected; consistent with endorphin release mediating placebo analgesia. Zubieta et al., J Neurosci 2005 (PMID 16120776): PET imaging in sustained pain, placebo activated mu-opioid receptor neurotransmission (rostral anterior cingulate, DLPFC, insula, nucleus accumbens), paralleled by lower pain ratings; expectation of relief modulates physical and emotional states. Benedetti, Carlino & Pollo, Neuropsychopharmacology 2011 (PMID 20592717): how placebos change the patient's brain. Angle: why fair trials compare against a placebo.

cards.html:
Placebo effect

A fake pill can make your brain release painkillers.

1978 · The Lancet

Wisdom-tooth surgery

Patients got a dummy drug. Some felt less pain.

The test

Then naloxone, which blocks opioid signals.

The relief vanished.

The answer

Endorphins

Your brain's own opioid peptides did the work.

2005 · J Neuroscience

Brain scans agree

A placebo switched on the opioid system. Pain dropped.

Why it matters

Fair trials need a placebo group.

Without one, almost anything looks like it works.

Save this for the next 'miracle' claim.
